 A low pressure area is inside PAR, 915 km east of Eastern Visayas. Pagasa has not named it or raised a wind signal
 A low pressure area entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility on Thursday, 915 kilometers east of Eastern Visayas, while Pagasa tracked Typhoon In-fa 3,540 kilometers away. No wind signals are up. Here is what the bureau has and has not said, and why Thursday's rain in Metro Manila comes from the shear line instead. #LowPressureArea #PAGASA #Weather #Philippines
 by 
 ASTIG PR 
 7 hours ago 7 hours ago 
 Advertisements 
 A low pressure area is now inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, 915 kilometers east of Eastern Visayas as of 8 a.m. on Thursday, October 29, 2026. It is close enough that Pagasa will be watching it daily. It is not close enough, yet, to have a name, a wind signal or a track.
 In its 10 a.m. outlook, Pagasa said the disturbance remained a low pressure area. The outlook also tracked Typhoon In-fa at 3,540 km east of Central Luzon, packing 175 kph winds
 Neither system made landfall on Thursday. What the outlook did was put the country back into a pattern it has been in for most of October, with one disturbance close enough to watch while the amihan season is already underway.
 This account uses only the figures in the bureau’s Thursday advisories, as carried by Inquirer.net . It will be updated if Pagasa names the system or issues a track.
 Where the low pressure area is, and what Pagasa has not said
 A low pressure area is a broad, loosely organized region of low atmospheric pressure. It often brings rain and gusty winds, and it can develop into a tropical depression, the first stage at which the Philippines names a cyclone. It can also fizzle out unnamed.
 Thursday’s outlook places the system east of Eastern Visayas, the region covering Samar, Leyte, Biliran and Eastern Samar. The outlook as reported states no direction of movement and no forecast intensity, and no province was placed under a wind signal.
 Monitoring time 
 8 a.m. and 10 a.m., Thursday, October 29, 2026 
 Low pressure area 
 915 kilometers east of Eastern Visayas, inside the Philippine Area of Responsibility 
 Typhoon In-fa 
 3,540 kilometers east of Central Luzon, outside the Philippine Area of Responsibility, 175 kph winds and 215 kph gusts 
 Wind signals 
 None raised as of the 10 a.m. outlook 
 Shear line rains 
 Metro Manila, Calabarzon, Aurora, Bicol Region, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Marinduque, Oriental Mindoro 
 Amihan 
 Cagayan Valley, Cordillera, Nueva Ecija 
 The rain forecast for Thursday comes from the shear line
 In its 5 a.m. forecast, Pagasa said a shear line will wet Metro Manila, Calabarzon, Aurora and the Bicol Region. The amihan will reach Cagayan Valley, Cordillera and Nueva Ecija
 That distinction matters for anyone travelling for Undas. The rains forecast over the capital region are attributed to the shear line, a boundary where the amihan’s cool air meets warmer air from the Pacific side, and not to the low pressure area still sitting off the Visayas. 
 A shear line can produce days of steady rain with no cyclone anywhere near the country. A low pressure area 915 kilometers offshore does the opposite: it is close enough to watch and far enough that, so far, it changes nothing on land.
 Why the ocean is being watched so closely this week
 The amihan season began this week, and Pagasa warned at its onset that a developing La Niña could turn the cool months into a wetter and flood-prone stretch, as this desk reported in the amihan onset story . A disturbance east of the Visayas in the first days of the amihan is the kind of setup forecasters track closest.
 October has already produced several. Typhoon Rosal crossed the northern Philippines in the third week of the month, carrying 12-meter seas off Batanes at one point before it left the area, and the bureau’s final bulletin on Rosal recorded 5.5-meter seas when it left.
 What an outlook does not justify
 A formation outlook is not a cyclone bulletin. Pagasa issues the latter, with a name, wind signals and a forecast track, only once a disturbance becomes a tropical depression. Until then the advice is the ordinary one for a rainy October: watch for localized flooding, keep an eye on class and work suspensions, and read the bureau’s own advisories instead of forecasts circulating on social media.
 The desk will report a name, a wind signal or a track if one is issued, and every figure here comes from Pagasa’s own Thursday advisories.
 (Photo: Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) at peak intensity east of the Philippines on November 7, 2013, from the Terra satellite. The frame is file imagery of a past storm and does not depict Thursday’s low pressure area, Typhoon In-fa, or any weather on October 29, 2026. Image: MODIS imagery from the Terra satellite, via Nasa EOSDIS Worldview, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons)
